About: Kepler's Laws from Newtonian Gravity

Source

Learning outcome
L37 — Kepler's three laws follow from Newton's law of gravity.
Simulation
Single orbital core with three law-modes (K1, K2, K3).
Concept
K1 orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus; K2 equal areas in equal times; K3 T² ∝ a³.
Misconception
Planets move at constant speed and heavier planets orbit slower. In fact, speed varies (K2), and period depends only on the semi-major axis a, not on planet mass (K3).
Inquiry
Orient to the ellipse → predict speed → equal areas → predict period vs mass → build T² vs a³.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Orient to the ellipse

K1 says a planet's orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. The empty focus is marked with ◆; the Sun sits at the other focus. Vary eccentricity to see the ellipse deform.

2 · Where is the planet fastest?

Watch the planet trace the ellipse. Where does it move fastest?

3 · Equal areas in equal times?

The animated planet sweeps out area continuously. Two windows accumulate the area actually swept over the same Δt: one across perihelion (orange), one across aphelion (cyan). Predict — do they enclose equal area?

A₁ (perihelion window)— AU²
A₂ (aphelion window)— AU²
A₁ / A₂—

4 · Does a heavier planet orbit slower?

The canvas now shows two planets on the same orbit — a light one (blue) and one 10× heavier (magenta). Watch: do they stay together, or does one lag?

5 · Build T² ∝ a³

Add at least two planets from the chip row. Each is integrated by Newton's law; its period is measured from perihelion crossings and plotted. Watch what shape the points make on the log–log plot.

Now predict — Jupiter orbits at a = 5.2 AU. Roughly what period do you expect?

From Newton to Kepler

The Physics

Kepler’s Laws from Newtonian Gravity · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

One planet circles the Sun, pulled by Newton's inverse-square gravity. The sim has three modes, K1, K2 and K3, and each one looks at one of Kepler's three laws.

What you'll learn

  • Where the Sun sits inside an elliptical orbit.
  • What changes and what stays the same as a planet goes round.
  • How the time for one lap is linked to the size of the orbit.
The orbit seen from above. The dotted line is the long axis. Not to scale.

What's on screen

  • The Sun: the yellow dot. The faint grey rings around it are 0.4 AU apart.
  • The planet: the blue dot, with a thin line to the Sun and a trail behind it. The ellipse is the solid outline.
  • The labels: the diamond marks the empty focus, a dotted line marks a, and perihelion and aphelion are named. Hide Text removes the labels.
See itStay in K1 with e = 0.60 and run at 0.25× speed. Watch for: the blue dot going round the ellipse once in about 8 s, with the Sun not at the centre and the ◆ marking the empty focus on the far side.

Units are AU, years and solar masses, so the Sun's pull is GM = 4π² AU³/yr². The Sun stays still and only the one planet (or each added planet) moves.

03

The orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus

This is Kepler's first law, mode K1. A pull toward the Sun that falls off as 1/r² makes a bound planet follow an ellipse. The Sun is at one focus, and the other focus is empty. The centre of the ellipse is not the Sun.

Two numbers describe the ellipse: the semi-major axis a, which here is 1 AU, and the eccentricity e. With θ measured from perihelion, the distance from the Sun is

r(θ) = a(1 − e²) / (1 + e cos θ)
Perihelion r = a(1 − e) at θ = 0°. Aphelion r = a(1 + e) at θ = 180°.

The foci are 2ae apart, which is 1.20 AU at e = 0.60, and e = 0 is a circle with the Sun at the centre. At e = 0.60 perihelion sits on the first grey ring and aphelion on the fourth.

ePerihelion a(1 − e)Aphelion a(1 + e)Short half-axis b
01.000 AU1.000 AU1.000 AU
0.600.400 AU1.600 AU0.800 AU
0.850.150 AU1.850 AU0.527 AU

Real planets are far rounder: Earth has e = 0.017 and Mercury, the most stretched in the sim's list, 0.206.

See itSet e to 0.85 in K1 and run at 0.25× speed. Watch for: a long thin ellipse, the ◆ far to the left, and the planet starting 0.15 AU from the Sun, inside the first grey ring.
04

The planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion

Gravity pulls the planet along the line to the Sun, so it speeds up as it falls in and slows as it climbs out. The next section shows that the angular momentum about the Sun cannot change. At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is at right angles to the radius, so that momentum per unit mass is just r v.

rp vp = ra va  ⟹  vp/va = (1 + e)/(1 − e)
The speed anywhere is v² = GM(2/r − 1/a).

The sim has no speed readout, so you judge it by how fast the dot moves. The planet starts at perihelion at its top speed.

Eccentricity ePerihelion speedAphelion speedRatio
06.283 AU/yr (29.8 km/s)6.283 AU/yr1
0.6012.566 AU/yr (59.6 km/s)3.142 AU/yr (14.9 km/s)4
0.8522.066 AU/yr (104.6 km/s)1.789 AU/yr (8.5 km/s)12.3

At e = 0 the speed never changes. For e = 0.60, the first quarter of the time takes the planet 148° round the Sun, and the next quarter only the last 32°.

See itStay in K1 with e = 0.60 and run at 0.25× speed. Watch for: the dot sweeping past the Sun's side in about 2 s and then crawling over the far end, reaching aphelion at about 4 s.
05

The line from the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times

This is Kepler's second law, mode K2. In a short time dt the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps a thin triangle of area dA = ½ r² dθ. Gravity has no turning effect about the Sun, so the angular momentum L stays fixed, and so does the rate:

dA/dt = L / 2m = constant
For a = 1 AU this is π√(1 − e²) AU² per year.

K2 measures two windows, each 0.10 of the orbit period long: an orange one across perihelion and a cyan one across aphelion. At e = 0.60 the orbit's area is πab = 2.513 AU², so each window sweeps 0.10 of it.

Window (0.1 yr each)Angle at the SunPath lengthArea swept
Perihelion144.7°1.17 AU0.2513 AU²
Aphelion11.3°0.32 AU0.2513 AU²

One wedge is short and wide, and the other long and thin. The time is the same and so is the area.

See itSwitch to K2, keep e = 0.60, and run at 0.25× speed. Watch for: a thin cyan wedge at the far end after about 4 s, then a short wide orange one near the Sun, then A₁ and A₂ both reading near 0.25 AU².
06

The planet's own mass cancels out of the orbit

Newton's second law sets the planet's m r̈ equal to the pull of gravity. The planet's mass m is on both sides.

m r̈ = −(GMm/r²) r̂  ⟹  r̈ = −(GM/r²) r̂
No m is left, so the path depends only on the start.

A planet 10 times heavier is pulled 10 times harder, but it also takes 10 times more force to change its motion. Started the same way, it follows the same orbit with the same lap time.

The sim integrates this equation, which has no m in it, so a 10× heavier planet lies exactly on the light one all the way round.

The Sun is treated as fixed here. In the real sky the Sun moves a little too, which gives T² = 4π²a³ / G(M + m). Even for Jupiter that changes T by only about 0.05%.

See itStay in K1 at e = 0.60 and add the heavy planet. Watch for: a magenta ring labelled "10× heavier (same orbit)" that stays on the blue dot for the whole lap.
07

The square of the period grows as the cube of the orbit's size

This is Kepler's third law, mode K3. The whole ellipse, area πab, is swept at the steady rate from K2, which gives Newton's form of the law:

T² = (4π²/GM) a³  ⟹  T² = a³  (T in years, a in AU)
Only a matters. The eccentricity and the planet's mass do not.

K3 measures each planet's period by timing its passes through perihelion, then plots T² against a³ on log axes. Points on the slope-1 line mean T² = a³. The T² / a³ readout averages the measured planets.

Planeta (AU)a³T = a3/2 (yr)
Mercury0.3870.0580.241
Earth1.0001.0001.000
Mars1.5243.5401.881
Jupiter5.203140.911.87
Saturn9.537867.429.45

Jupiter is 5.2 times farther out than Earth, yet its year is 11.87 times longer. A period that grew in step with distance would give 5.2 years, and one that grew as distance squared would give 27.

See itSwitch to K3 and add Earth, Mars and Jupiter. Watch for: three points on the dashed slope-1 line and T² / a³ reading 1.000, with Jupiter measured last.
08

Where it matters

  • Weighing the Sun. Earth has a = 1 AU and T = 1 yr, so GM = 4π²a³/T² = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s². One planet's orbit gives the Sun's mass.
  • Earth's seasons. Earth has e = 0.017, so it is 147.1 million km from the Sun in early January and 152.1 million km in July. Its speed varies by about 3.5% over the year. The tilt of its axis, not this distance, causes the seasons.
  • Comets. Halley's comet has a = 17.8 AU and e = 0.967. Its period is 17.83/2 ≈ 75 years, and it is about 60 times faster at perihelion than at aphelion. That is beyond the sim's e = 0.85 limit.
  • Satellites. A moon or a satellite round any body obeys T² ∝ a³, with that body's GM in place of the Sun's.
  • Real limits. The sim has one planet, a fixed Sun and no pull between planets. Real orbits also tilt and drift slowly.
09

Summary

In one line. Newton's inverse-square gravity accounts for all three of Kepler's laws.

Key points

  • K1: r(θ) = a(1 − e²)/(1 + e cos θ), with the Sun at one focus.
  • The speed is greatest at perihelion, and vp/va = (1 + e)/(1 − e).
  • K2: dA/dt = L/2m is constant, so equal times sweep equal areas.
  • K3: T² = 4π²a³/GM, which is T² = a³ in years and AU. The planet's mass does not enter.

Common mix-ups

  • "The planet moves at a constant speed." Only for e = 0. At e = 0.60 it is 4 times faster at perihelion than at aphelion.
  • "Heavier planets orbit more slowly." The planet's mass cancels, so the orbit and period do not depend on it.
  • "The Sun is at the centre of the ellipse." It is at one focus. The centre is a distance ae away, and the other focus is empty.

Things to try on your own

  • Set e = 0 and watch the speed stay steady. Then raise e.
  • In K2, set e = 0.85. The aphelion wedge turns into a sliver, yet A₁ / A₂ stays near 1.
  • In K3, add all seven planets and watch T² / a³.
